full_judgment:
12. The accused was thereafter examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to which he reiterated his plea of innocence. He further stated his signature was obtained by force. He, of course, refused to adduce any evidence. 

 14. Mr Anisul Huq, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant with Mr ABM Golam Majid, submits that 3 witnesses being prima facie independent witnesses shown as attesting witnesses of the seizure list did not corroborate the prosecution case and, as such, the recovery of the arms and ammunition from the possession of the accused appellant has not been proved at all. It is submitted further that the alleged place of occurrence being not under the control of accused appellant and there being no evidence whatsoever that the accused appellant kept or concealed the arms and ammunition at the place of occurrence the order of conviction is illegal. It is further stated that the evidence of PWs 1-3 if excluded from consideration the remaining witnesses being members of the Police personnel are highly interested and, as such, on their testimony the accused-appellant cannot be convicted. More so, the learned Advocate submits, that the evidence of those witnesses ie PWs 4-8 is also full of contradictions and, as such, the impugned judgment cannot be maintained. 

 15. Mr Shueb Ahmed, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the State, on the other hand, submits that though PWs 1-3 did not corroborate the prosecution case but evidence of other witnesses namely, PWs 4-8 being cogent and trustworthy the impugned judgment is maintainable in law. He further submits that there is no enmity between the said witnesses and the accused and, as such, there is no reason whatsoever to disbelieve their testimony and hence the impugned judgment cannot be assailed. 

 16. We have considered the submissions made at the Bar and perused the materials including the evidence. It appears that the prosecution though produced 8 witnesses but PWs 1, 2 and 3 being attesting witnesses of the seizure list did not support the prosecution version as to recovery of the arms and ammunition from the possession of the accused appellant. The learned Assistant Attorney General in this connection referred to the decision in the case of Abul BasIzar Shaikh vs State reported in 51 DLR 252 referring to paragraph 8 submits that the seizure list witnesses in the said case were declared hostile by the prosecution but relying on evidence of other witnesses the order of conviction was upheld in the said case. In this connection decision in the case of Abdur Rezzak Talukder vs State reported in 51 DLR 83 may be referred to wherein it has been observed 

 17. In this connection another decision in the case of Abul Hashem Master vs State reported in 44 DLR 159 also may be referred to wherein it was argued on behalf of the appellant in a case where the accused was convicted under Arms Act that the witnesses except PWs 4 and 5 are Police personnel and their evidence should be taken with a grain of salt. Though ultimately the accused was acquitted in the said case on other grounds but it was held "There is no reason why the evidence of the Police personnel should be discarded simply because they belonged to police force when they came before the court and testified to the occurrence. They were fully cross-examined. Their evidence is the evidence within the meaning of section 3 of the Evidence Act. It cannot also be said that these witnesses are interested or inimically disposed towards the accused-appellant." It may further be stated that even in a case of non-examination of seizure list witness the order of conviction if otherwise found to be valid cannot be interfered with. In this connection the case of Mahbubur Rahman Khan alias 7ipu is State reported in 16 BLD (AD) 268 may be referred to wherein no seizure list witness of the revolver was examined but it was held that there being other circumstances, non-examination of any men of public and seizure list witnesses was not at all material and ultimately the order of conviction was affirmed dismissing the appeal. 

 19. The next point agitated by the appellant was the manner of the recovery of the arms and ammunition. The manner has been seriously challenged by the appellant drawing our attention to the contradictions of the prosecution witnesses themselves specifically those witnesses who have been relied on by the prosecution namely, PWs 4-8. PW 4 constable Haroon stated that Bilu being arrested on 14-4-90 at about 1-10 PM at night he was taken to the police station where he admitted to have arms and ammunition in his possession but PW 6 Shantanu the Officer of the police station stated that the accused was arrested on 15-4-90 from Arabpur bus stand. It appears from the evidence of PW 4 that he deposed that the revolver and ammunition were recovered which were kept hidden under earth beneath a sishu tree and in cross-examination he stated that with the help of a Shabol by digging earth the revolver was recovered and that the shabol was taken from person by which accused Bilu himself by digging the earth brought out the revolver and the ammunition. But PW 5 constable Idris Ali in his evidence does not corroborate PW 4 as to digging earth by shabol. He rather belies PW 4 deposing ইট দিয়া অস্ত্র ঢাকা ছিল It. therefore, appears that PW 4 has been contradicted by PW 5 on this point. PW 6 the officer-in-charge of police, informant of the case, himself deposed that there was no hole near the sishu tree and only two pieces of bricks were there covering the arms and ammunition, 

 It further appears that PW 4 stated that they went to the place of occurrence at 12-30 at night on foot but PW 5 in cross-examination stated that they went there by truck of the police line Similarly, PW 6 also stated that they went there by police truck. We have already noticed that the defence suggested that the informant party did not at all go to the place. In view of the aforesaid discussions it appears that the witnesses PWs 4-8 even did not corroborate each other as to the manner of the occurrence ie as to recovery of the arms and ammunition from the possession of the accused-appellant. PW 8 stated that there was no case registered against the accused appellant for any occurrence on 2-4-90 and that he mentioned some cases against the accused but he could not remember whether the case was of mass upsurge of 1982. It further appears that there is no evidence as to any occurrence of 2-4-90 in which the accused is alleged to have created a reign of terror by firing from his unauthorised revolver or extorting tolls, etc. 

 21. Be that as it may, none of the witnesses deposed that the accused himself kept the arms and ammunition at the place of occurrence or that he had exclusive possession over that spot or that none else had access to the spot. Moreover, PW 8 SI Nurul Islam who not only investigated the case but also accompanied informant to the place of occurrence at the time of recovery of the arms and ammunition deposed that there are other houses nearby so there is easy access of person and that the place was under the control of the College. In such view of the matter even if the accused had any knowledge of the arms and ammunition lying at the spot pointed out by him, it cannot bring the accused within the mischief of section 19 of the Arms Act. In this connection the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant referred to the decision in the case of Arshadullah vs State reported in 21 DLR 684 and Nurul Islam vs State 1988 BLD 106 while considering the case of accused Nurul Islam, who was convicted under section 19(a) and 19(f) of the Arms Act. The witnesses deposed that the appellant Nurul Islam and another namely, Arshadullah led them to a panboraj near his house and pointed out spots from where two incriminating articles namely, gun and cartridges were recovered and that the appellant could not produce any licence. It was further found that there was no evidence against appellant Nurul Islam to connect him with the possession of those incriminating articles or with the use of the gun at any time and that there was also no evidence to show that the places from which those articles were recovered were in exclusive possession of the appellant and/or inaccessible to others. With the above finding appeal of appellant Nurul Islam was allowed and conviction and sentence passed against him were set aside. 

 22. In view of the discussions made above it appears that the prosecution could not prove beyond shadow of doubt the charge against the accused appellant and, as such, he is entitled to the benefit of doubt. We have perused the impugned judgment passed by the special tribunal. After discussing the evidence of witnesses the tribunal relying on the decision reported in 1988 BLD 106 dealt at length regarding the provision of search as contemplated under section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and made the finding that from the evidence of witnesses it had been proved that the arms and ammunition were recovered from the place of occurrence being pointed out by the accused. In the discussion of the evidence we have stated the contradictions in the evidence of the witnesses as to the manner of the alleged occurrence. It appears that the tribunal passed impugned judgment disregarding the aforesaid facts and circumstances including contradictions in the evidence of the witnesses and thus passed the impugned judgment and order. On the reasons aforesaid we find that the impugned judgment calls for our interference and we are of the view that the appeal has substance.
